abstract: The imposter phenomenon (or imposterism) is a commonly reported psychological pattern in which individuals persistently doubt their abilities and accomplishments despite objective evidence of their competence. Imposterism is associated with chronic self-doubt and reduced well-being, yet its cognitive mechanisms remain unclear. In a large online sample (N = 602), we investigated how self-reported imposter feelings relate to decision-making, confidence and information search in a perceptual decision-making task. Imposterism was associated with lower confidence in perceptual decisions and increased information seeking, despite not being associated with any detriment in objective perceptual performance. Though symptoms of anxiety and depression contributed to the relationship between imposterism and confidence, imposterism uniquely predicted increased information-seeking. Interestingly, the increased information seeking associated with imposterism did not lead to an imposterism-specific increase in final decision performance and did not alleviate overall uncertainty: imposterism remained associated with reduced confidence even for final decisions. To explain this, we hypothesised that information seeking may compensate for maladaptive second-guessing. Supporting this, imposterism predicted greater response switching and decreases in accuracy on trials where no additional information was sought, reflecting counterproductive changes of mind. These effects were absent on trials where information was accessed, suggesting that seeking additional information helped buffer against maladaptive second-guessing. Overall, our findings show that imposterism is marked by low confidence, heightened information seeking, and vulnerability to second-guessing in the absence of external reassurance. These results provide novel insights into distortions of self-evaluation in imposterism and highlight a compensatory role for information seeking in stabilising performance. Our study advances understanding of a widely discussed yet underexplored psychological phenomenon with significant implications for education, workplace wellbeing, and mental health.
